### tgv2d

The `tgv2d` example demonstrates UQ for a two-dimensional Taylor--Green vortex problem with an uncertain initial velocity field.
Unlike the other examples of this category, this case features a multi-dimensional uncertain initial value problem, where the uncertainty is introduced through a four-dimensional random perturbation in the initial condition.
Specifically, the velocity field is modified as $u_0^R = u_0 + \epsilon_d(x, y)$, where the perturbation $\epsilon_d$ is constructed from a truncated Fourier expansion with first-order harmonics.
The perturbation takes the form

$$
\epsilon_d(x, y) = \frac{1}{4} \sum_{(i, j) \in \{0,1\}^2} \delta_{d,i,j} \, \alpha_i(4x) \, \alpha_j(4y),
$$

where $\delta_{d,i,j} \sim \mathcal{U}(-0.025, 0.025)$ are i.i.d. random amplitudes, and

$$
\alpha_i(x) =
\begin{cases}
\sin(x), & \text{if } i = 0, \\
\cos(x), & \text{if } i = 1.
\end{cases}
$$

These four random amplitudes are defined via separate uniform distributions and combined into a single joint distribution:

```{.cpp}
// Define uniform distributions for each harmonic amplitude
auto perturb1 = uniform(-0.025, 0.025);
auto perturb2 = uniform(-0.025, 0.025);
auto perturb3 = uniform(-0.025, 0.025);
auto perturb4 = uniform(-0.025, 0.025);

// Create a 4D joint distribution
auto jointPerturb = joint<T>({perturb1, perturb2, perturb3, perturb4});
```

This setup creates a four-dimensional uncertain parameter space.
Both Monte Carlo sampling and the stochastic collocation method can be used to propagate the uncertainty through the simulation.
As in the other examples, quantities of interest -- such as kinetic energy -- can be collected across samples and analyzed using built-in statistical tools.
Postprocessing can be performed via $\OpenLB$'s built-in functions to compute and visualize the mean and standard deviation of the flow field, providing insights into how initial condition uncertainties evolve over time (see @fig-uqTgv).
